clue.text: Frequent ups and downs in my line of work

definitions.text: Frequent ups and downs in my line of work

parts.words: Frequent ups and downs in my line of work
parts.note: read as a career full of mood swings, but literally a job of riding up and down floors all day in an elevator car

explanation.surface: Someone complains that their job is an emotional rollercoaster.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'ups and downs' sound like changing fortunes, but they are the literal trips of an old-style elevator operator.
explanation.definitionFit: An attendant who operated a lift spent the working day travelling up and down between floors.

clue.text: Girl's not top of the form

indicators.note: not top of says the first letter of the word is removed

parts.note: a form is a school class

explanation.surface: A girl is not top of her class at school.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not top of' drops the C from CLASS, a school form.
explanation.definitionFit: A lass is a young woman or girl, chiefly in Scottish and northern English usage.

clue.text: Charge about in battle

indicators.note: in places the word for about inside the word for battle

parts.note: a fight is a battle
re means about, concerning

explanation.surface: An accusation concerning conduct during combat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Charge' looks like an accusation or attack, but it is the fee for carrying goods.
explanation.definitionFit: Freight is the cost paid for transporting goods, a charge for carriage.

clue.text: Painter getting up mid-morning?

indicators.note: getting up in a down clue means the letters rise, read from bottom to top

parts.note: ten o'clock in the morning, written ten a.m., is the middle of the morning

explanation.surface: An artist who rises halfway through the morning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mid-morning' is TEN AM; 'getting up' reverses it in this down clue. Édouard Manet was a French painter.
explanation.definitionFit: Édouard Manet was a French Impressionist artist, a painter.

clue.text: Beginner, nervous one, has struggle to be heard

indicators.note: nervous suggests the letters of one are jittery and so rearranged
to be heard says the word is spoken, its sound used rather than its spelling

parts.note: a fight is a struggle

explanation.surface: A nervous novice has a battle to make themselves heard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nervous' rearranges ONE to NEO; 'to be heard' gives the sound of FIGHT, spelt PHYTE.
explanation.definitionFit: A neophyte is a novice or new convert, someone just starting out.

clue.text: Back out of race, having superficial injury

definitions.meaning: to withdraw a horse or competitor from an event before it starts
a shallow mark or graze on the skin

explanation.surface: An athlete pulls out of a race because of a minor wound.
explanation.definitionFit: Withdrawing an entrant is called scratching it, and a light graze from a claw is also so called.

clue.text: Don't go to bed before completion of various exercises

parts.note: to sit up is to stay up and not go to bed

indicators.note: completion of points at the final letter of the following word

explanation.surface: Someone stays up late to finish a variety of workouts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'completion of' takes the last letter of 'various'.
explanation.definitionFit: Raising the torso from lying to sitting is a standard abdominal workout move.

clue.text: Model T Ford — a car for showing driving skill

indicators.note: model as a verb means to shape, so the letters are moulded into a new form

explanation.surface: A Model T Ford is the car for demonstrating how well you drive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Model T Ford' looks like the famous car, but 'Model' rearranges T FORD A CAR.
explanation.definitionFit: Roadcraft is the competence and judgement a motorist uses on the road.

clue.text: No longer going out together, it's clear

definitions.meaning: of a couple, finished with each other
out the other side, as in being clear of something

explanation.surface: A couple's romance is plainly over.
explanation.definitionFit: A couple who have split are finished with each other, and someone past an obstacle has come out of it.

clue.text: A seat in the stalls for this movie?

definitions.text: A seat in the stalls for this movie?

parts.words: A seat in the stalls for this movie?
parts.note: stalls looks like cinema seating, but they are stable stalls, where a seat would be on a mount, fitting a western

explanation.surface: Someone asks about booking a stalls seat for a film.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stalls' suggests cinema seating; in stables, the seat is a saddle, so the film is a western.
explanation.definitionFit: A western film full of cowboys riding is nicknamed this, mocking it as a melodrama on mounts.

clue.text: Tough job getting a supporter on board

parts.note: stern means tough or severe
a post is a job or position

explanation.surface: A hard job comes with someone backing you up on the committee.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On board' suggests a committee, but here it means aboard ship: the timber at the back of a vessel that supports the rudder.
explanation.definitionFit: This upright timber at a ship's rear holds up the rudder, a structural support aboard a vessel.

clue.text: Fellow leaves lighter-coloured frame

indicators.note: the word leaves says the fellow departs from the longer word, so its letter is taken out

parts.note: fairer means paler or lighter in colour

explanation.surface: A man departs from a paler picture frame.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leaves' takes F (fellow) out of FAIRER. An airer is a British household rack for drying clothes.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a wooden or metal rack, a framework on which washing is hung to dry.

clue.text: See what art thief intends to do

definitions.meaning: to understand or grasp a situation

definitions.text: what art thief intends to do
definitions.meaning: read literally, someone stealing art plans to take a painting

explanation.surface: An explanation of an art thief's plans.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to understand, while literally a painting thief aims to grab a canvas.

clue.text: Grant needed to study whole term at university being discussed?

indicators.note: being discussed means being talked about, so the words are spoken and their sound used

parts.note: to con is an old word meaning to study; a session is the full academic term or year at a university

explanation.surface: A student grant is needed for a full term of university study.
explanation.walkthrough: 'being discussed' says CON plus SESSION is heard, not spelt.
explanation.definitionFit: A concession is something granted or allowed, as in a privilege yielded.

clue.text: Survives Open University finals, securing first in theology

indicators.note: securing means holding something firmly inside, so a letter is held within the other pieces

parts.note: OU is the abbreviation for the Open University, the UK distance-learning university
lasts means final ones

indicators.note: first in points at the opening letter of the following word

explanation.surface: Someone makes it through their Open University final exams, having come top in theology.
explanation.walkthrough: 'finals' is a noun here, final ones, not exams; 'securing' and 'first in' wedge the theology initial between the university and the finals.
explanation.definitionFit: To outlive or last longer than something is to survive it.

clue.text: Smile suppressed by a head displaying wrath

indicators.note: suppressed by means held down inside, so the smile is enclosed by the other pieces

parts.note: a ness is a headland
a grin is a smile

explanation.surface: Someone stifles a smile in front of an angry boss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'head' looks like a boss but is a headland, a common crossword usage; 'suppressed by' holds the smile inside the other pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Being furious, displaying rage, is the state of anger.

clue.text: In some matches, remains to count takings

indicators.note: in says one piece goes inside the other, the remains placed within the matches

parts.note: a cup is a competition made up of a series of matches
ash is what remains after burning

explanation.surface: During some games, a shopkeeper stays behind to count the money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'matches' suggests the things you strike, which makes 'remains' look like their ash; it is, but the matches are a CUP competition.
explanation.definitionFit: To total up the money taken at the end of a day's trading is a British idiom for counting the takings.

clue.text: Climbing uncultivated land, husband noticed a bog across the pond

indicators.note: climbing in a down clue means the letters go upwards, read in reverse

parts.note: a moor is open uncultivated land
saw means noticed

explanation.surface: Climbing over wild moorland, a husband spotted a marsh in America.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Climbing' reverses MOOR, H and SAW together. 'bog' is British slang for toilet and 'across the pond' means in America, so a bog is a toilet there.
explanation.definitionFit: In American English this is the polite word for a toilet, which a Briton might call the bog.

clue.text: Sticky part for recycling? Yes

indicators.note: part says only a portion of the following words is wanted, a run inside them

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a gummy item goes in the recycling, and is told yes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'part' points at a run of letters inside 'recycling? Yes', which spans the two words.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that adheres or clings is sticky.

clue.text: Think CO should be replaced by one who's in the know

annotationWithheld.why: Think CO should be replaced by one who's in the know (7): CONSIDER with CO replaced by I gives the answer, but 'one' must be both the I and part of the definition 'one who's in the know'
annotationWithheld.clue: Think CO should be replaced by one who's in the know

clue.text: Can people spend a lot of time here with ponies?

definitions.text: Can people spend a lot of time here with ponies?

parts.words: Can people spend a lot of time here with ponies?
parts.note: reads as a question about a riding holiday, but can is slang for prison, and this moorland in Devon has a famous jail and wild ponies

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether you can have a long pony-trekking holiday somewhere.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Can' looks like 'are able to', but it is slang for prison: the Devon moor has a well-known prison and wild ponies.
explanation.definitionFit: This Devon upland holds a long-stay prison for convicts and is famous for its free-roaming ponies.

clue.text: A certain contractor's outbreak of ego and bile

indicators.note: outbreak of suggests the letters burst out and scatter into a new order

explanation.surface: A builder has a sudden flare-up of conceit and bad temper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'outbreak of' rearranges EGO and BILE. The 's is short for 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: An obligee is the party to a contract to whom an obligation is owed.

clue.text: A country of old, miles away

annotationWithheld.why: A country of old, miles away (6): definition 'A country of old' is clear, but no parse of 'miles away' builds the letters; the scan prints it so and a search found nothing
annotationWithheld.clue: A country of old, miles away

clue.text: Latin speech is misinterpreted in Vatican building

indicators.note: misinterpreted says the letters of the preceding words are taken in the wrong way and rearranged

explanation.surface: A Latin speech is misunderstood inside a Vatican building.
explanation.walkthrough: 'misinterpreted' rearranges LATIN SPEECH IS.
explanation.definitionFit: The papal chapel in Vatican City, famed for Michelangelo's ceiling, is a building of the Vatican.

clue.text: Stout-hearted pair, rather sickly looking

indicators.note: hearted says something forms the heart of the other word, sitting in its middle

parts.note: stout is a dark beer, a kind of ale

explanation.surface: A brave couple are looking rather unwell.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stout-hearted' reads as brave; it puts ALE (stout) in the heart of PR (pair).
explanation.definitionFit: Paler means more pallid or wan, like someone who appears somewhat ill.

clue.text: Rising in the night, perhaps, along with others

indicators.note: rising in a down clue means the letters go upward, read in reverse

parts.note: late can mean in the night, as in late hours

explanation.surface: Getting up during the night, maybe, together with other people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rising' reverses LATE in this down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin abbreviation 'et al.' means 'and others', used in citations.

clue.text: Cease backing popular record company

indicators.note: backing here means coming behind, so the word for cease follows the word for popular

parts.note: in means popular or fashionable
to die is to cease

explanation.surface: Stop supporting a well-liked record label.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backing' looks like support or a reversal, but it places DIE behind IN.
explanation.definitionFit: An independent label, a small record company outside the majors, is known by this short name.

clue.text: Draw attention to offence involving large sum of money

indicators.note: involving means taking in or enclosing, so the money sits inside the offence

parts.note: a slight is an insult or offence
a pot is a large sum of money, as in pots of cash

explanation.surface: Publicise an insult concerning a huge amount of cash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'involving' puts the money inside the offence; 'Draw attention to' is a verb, so the answer is read as a verb too.
explanation.definitionFit: To shine a beam on something, figuratively, is to highlight it and make people notice it.

clue.text: Portia's maid making comeback as temptress

indicators.note: making comeback says the whole run of letters is turned around and read backwards

parts.note: a siren is a seductive temptress

explanation.surface: An actress who played a servant returns to the stage as a seductress.
explanation.walkthrough: 'making comeback' turns AS SIREN back to front. In Shakespeare's The Merchant of Venice, Portia's waiting-woman is named Nerissa.
explanation.definitionFit: In The Merchant of Venice, the heroine's waiting-woman and confidante bears this name.

clue.text: Wonder if line's by this poet

parts.note: to marvel is to wonder
L is the abbreviation for line

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether a certain line was written by a particular poet.
explanation.walkthrough: Andrew Marvell was a 17th-century English poet.
explanation.definitionFit: Andrew Marvell wrote To His Coy Mistress, so he is a poet, the one referred to here.
